prompt.context: Our client is a large international software technology provider. News has just surfaced that the US Congress is preparing to pass a bill that will take effect in 6 months and will legalize unmanned, self-driving cars and trucks, as long as the vehicles do not carry any passengers. Our client is one of two vendors that, within this window, will be poised to deliver the Simultaneous Localization and Mapping Technology (SLAM software) which is needed to operate any and all self-driving vehicles. Their only competitive vendor is a large international computer chip manufacturer. While there are many technologies that enable self-driving cars to work, we are only focused on the mapping and car intelligence software, known as SLAM. SLAM software runs in the cloud, meaning that it runs on large servers connected to the internet and not on the vehicles themselves.
prompt.question: The client has contacted us to propose the best go-to-market strategy for their SLAM technology. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: How does the SLAM solution work technically?
clarifying_info.a: It is not important to know the technical details; it is a software program that runs on internet servers.

clarifying_info.q: Are other technologies for self-driving cars ready?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all other technologies besides SLAM are also expected to be ready for sale at the time the legislation passes.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to retrofit a vehicle to work with SLAM?
clarifying_info.a: The marginal cost to retrofit a vehicle to work with SLAM is assumed to be negligible discounted over the life of the vehicle.

exhibits.title: Fleet Size Distribution by Customer Segment
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the number of companies by fleet size across three customer segments: Large Interstate Freight, Cross State Mail and Package Delivery, and Last Mile Drop-Off Services
exhibits.data: Vast majority of companies have fewer than 10 vehicles; company count decreases as fleet size increases; Interstate segment has a larger proportion of bigger fleets compared to the other two segments

exhibits.title: Driver Labor Data by Segment
exhibits.shows: A table showing hours worked per week, hourly wages, and weeks worked per year for drivers in each of the three customer segments
exhibits.data: Last Mile: 30 hrs/week, $10/hr, 50 weeks/year; Cross State: 40 hrs/week, $15/hr, 50 weeks/year; Interstate: 50 hrs/week, $20/hr, 50 weeks/year

framework: Customers: Identify customer segments (logistics companies by fleet type), estimate number of vehicles per segment, and assess willingness to pay based on current driver labor costs
Competitor: Analyze the only other SLAM vendor (large chip manufacturer) — their pricing, product specs, shelf life, and addressable market
Client: Determine optimal go-to-market model (hardware sale vs. software license), cost structure, pricing, and expected revenue and profit

questions.prompt: Who are the potential customer segments and what do you know about their fleets?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify logistics-oriented segments since no passengers are allowed. The three segments are: Large Interstate Freight, Cross State Mail and Package Delivery, and Last Mile Drop-Off (e.g., Amazon Fresh-style warehouse-to-door delivery). Candidate should note that most companies have small fleets (<10 vehicles) and that interstate companies have a higher proportion of large fleets.

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual cost per driver for each segment to estimate willingness to pay.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply hours per week by hourly wage to get weekly wages, then multiply by weeks per year to get annual wages. This serves as a proxy for the savings — and thus willingness to pay — per vehicle license.

math.answer: Last Mile: $15,000/yr; Cross State: $30,000/yr; Interstate: $50,000/yr per driver replaced

questions.prompt: The competitor plans to sell their SLAM hardware device for $14.4 million; each unit supports up to 500 vehicles and has a shelf life of 4 years. What is the minimum fleet size needed to justify this purchase in each segment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first annualize the competitor price ($14.4M / 4 years = $3.6M/year), then divide by annual savings per driver to find the breakeven fleet size. This reveals that the vast majority of the market is priced out.

math.setup: Annual cost of competitor device = $14.4M / 4 years = $3.6M/year. Breakeven fleet size = Annual device cost / Annual savings per driver
math.answer: A company needs at least 240 vehicles (Last Mile), 120 vehicles (Cross State), or 72 vehicles (Interstate) to break even on the competitor product. Since most companies have fewer than 10 vehicles, the competitor's hardware model prices out the vast majority of the market.

questions.prompt: Our client's device costs $14 million to make and supports up to 1,000 vehicles. Its shelf life is 4 years at 50% capacity (500 vehicles) or 1 year at 100% capacity (1,000 vehicles). Since the client is a software company, they can sell per-vehicle annual software licenses instead of the physical device, running it from their datacenter at a cost of $1,000 per vehicle per year. What is the client's cost per vehicle license per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the software licensing model is a key differentiator vs. the competitor's hardware model. At 50% capacity (500 vehicles, 4-year life), the per-vehicle annual cost is: $14M device cost amortized over 4 years across 500 vehicles = $7,000/vehicle/year, plus $1,000 variable support = $8,000 total. However, the candidate in the casebook uses a simplified calculation: $14M / 1,000 vehicles = $14,000 setup cost per vehicle (one-time hardware allocated per vehicle slot), plus $1,000 annual support = $15,000 total cost per vehicle. Both approaches highlight that the cost is well below the $30,000 cross-state driver wage, enabling a strong margin.

math.setup: Client device cost allocated per vehicle slot + annual support cost per vehicle
steps: Hardware cost per vehicle slot: $14,000,000 / 1,000 vehicles = $14,000
math.answer: $15,000 per vehicle (total cost), yielding ~50% gross margin at a $30,000 license price

questions.prompt: What pricing strategy and target price would you recommend, and what are the expected revenue and profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend pricing just below the annual driver cost for the cross-state segment ($30,000) to capture both Cross State and Interstate markets while excluding the unprofitable Last Mile segment. At ~$30,000, the margin is ~50% ($30K price vs. $15K cost). At the forecasted 20,000 licenses sold across the two segments, revenue is $600M and profit is $300M.

math.setup: Revenue = licenses sold x price per license; Profit = (price - cost) x licenses sold
steps: Recommended price: just under $30,000 per vehicle license per year
math.answer: ~$600M in revenue and ~$300M in profit at ~50% margin

brainstorming.prompt: What additional pricing and market strategies should the client explore as next steps?

categories.name: Price Discrimination
ideas: Charge Interstate customers closer to $50,000 (their driver savings) rather than $30,000 to extract more value
Offer tiered pricing by segment or fleet size
Bundle additional features for higher-paying segments

categories.name: Fleet Size Optimization
ideas: Model the ideal vehicle load per server to extend shelf life and reduce cost per vehicle
Offer volume discounts for large fleets to capture the biggest customers at highest total revenue

categories.name: Market Expansion
ideas: Target Last Mile segment with a stripped-down, lower-cost product tier if costs can be reduced
Explore international markets where SLAM legislation may follow the US

categories.name: Competitive Moat
ideas: Lock in customers with multi-year contracts before the competitor can respond
Build switching costs through data network effects (mapping data improves with more vehicles)
Pursue partnerships with OEMs or logistics platforms to embed SLAM as the default standard

recommendation: Recommend the client sell individual vehicle software licenses priced just under $30,000 per vehicle per year, targeting the Interstate and Cross State segments
This pricing yields approximately 50% gross margin and an addressable market of ~20,000 licenses, translating to over $600M in revenue and $300M in profit

The software licensing model is a key differentiator versus the competitor's hardware device, making the solution accessible to the vast majority of the market that cannot afford the $14.4M hardware alternative
risks: Competitor could pivot to a software/SaaS model and undercut pricing
Legislation may be delayed or amended, shrinking the 6-month window to capture the market
Vehicle capacity assumptions (50% vs. 100% utilization) significantly affect server shelf life and true cost per vehicle
next_steps: Run sensitivity analysis to find the profit-maximizing price point across segments
Model price discrimination strategies to capture more value from Interstate customers (WTP ~$50,000)
Analyze optimal server utilization rates and fleet size mix to minimize cost per vehicle
